chunks: Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) said:
There is no affliction that descends upon a believing servant, but that God Mighty and Majestic inspires him to supplicate, except that the removal of that affliction would be imminent;
and there is no affliction that descends upon a believing servant, but that he withholds himself from supplication, except that affliction would be prolonged.
So whenever affliction descends, you must turn to supplication and humble pleading to God Mighty and Majestic.

key_terms.التَّضَرُّعِ: humble pleading — a form of du'a characterized by humility and earnestness
key_terms.بَلَاء: affliction/trial — a divine test sent to the believer, not merely misfortune
key_terms.كَشْف: removal/lifting — the divine act of ending the affliction
key_terms.وَشِيكاً: imminently/soon — the quick resolution of affliction when du'a is made
key_terms.يُلْهِمُهُ: inspires him — God placing the impulse for supplication in the believer's heart

ai.seo_question: What does Imam al-Kazim say about the relationship between supplication (du'a) and the lifting of affliction?
ai.summary: Imam Musa al-Kazim (peace be upon him) teaches that when God inspires a believer to supplicate during affliction, relief comes swiftly; but when the believer withholds from supplication, the affliction persists. This hadith was transmitted by Abu Wallad and establishes a direct correlation between du'a and divine relief, urging believers to embrace supplication as their primary response to trials. The teaching reflects the Shia theological principle that God's mercy is always accessible through sincere du'a, and that divine inspiration toward prayer is itself a sign of God's grace.
